current_article.identity: Lindemann and Stolz (2018), The Muslim Employment Gap, Human Capital, and Ethno-Religious Penalties: Evidence from Switzerland; 10.17645/si.v6i2.1395
current_article.reviewed: Methods 4.1–4.3; complete Findings 5.1–5.2 including Table 1/Table 2/Figure 1; introduction, relevant theory, conclusions and references
current_article.data: 2014 FSO Language, Religion and Culture Survey; initial N=16487 permanent residents 15+; labour-force selection ages 16–64 N=11012 (694 Muslims, 10318 non-Muslims); regression complete cases N=10916 (682, 10234).
current_article.actual_perceived_discrimination_comparis: Results 5.1 state 16% of Muslims versus 8% of non-Muslims felt discriminated against in the preceding 12 months; the next paragraph compares these descriptive findings jointly with both Gianni citations. The paragraph also covers education, language, migration, citizenship and religiosity: the plural comparison does not isolate discrimination alone. It is an empirical descriptive comparison, separate from the unemployment regressions.
current_article.discrimination_measure_limit: No personal discrimination variable enters the unemployment explanatory analysis. Exact question wording and attribution specifically to religion are not supplied for this descriptive variable. Do not equate it automatically with objectively measured hiring discrimination or religious-only discrimination.
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Table 1 reports 0.186 for Muslims and 0.079 for non-Muslims, conflicting with the prose 16% versus 8%; both retained without correction.

Theory 3.5 attributes religious discrimination in past 12 months to 21% Turks, 31% North Africans and 15% ex-Yugoslavians in Gianni 2015. This is an ethnicity-specific religious-discrimination claim, not the same numerical contrast as current Results.
The paper explicitly designs its employment-model comparison around Connor and Koenig; that fact alone does not erase the separate descriptive comparison to both Gianni reports.

original_2010_gris.identity: Vie musulmane en Suisse. Profils identitaires, demandes et perceptions des musulmans en Suisse; Matteo Gianni with named collaborators; May 2010 second edition.
original_2010_gris.observations: 30 semi-structured interviews purposively selected using four identity-profile categories. Appendix 2 describes 16 women/14 men, 14 French-language/16 German-language interviews; mixed nationalities and cantons. Census 1970–2000 used separately for structural context.
original_2010_gris.timeframe: Core study already published in 2005; 2010 preface explicitly says remainder reused unchanged, with additional contemporary analysis by Stéphane Lathion. Exact interview field dates not established from inspected text; no claim that interviews were collected in 2010.
original_2010_gris.perceived_discrimination_finding: Interviewees report prejudice, exclusion and discrimination, sometimes experienced personally and sometimes via acquaintances. Section 4.1.2.2 expressly cannot measure prevalence. Positive general accounts of integration coexist with accounts of discrimination. No representative Muslim versus non-Muslim 12-month numerical contrast established.

original_2015_book_and_chain.identity_correction: Original repository/publisher extract says Les musulmans en Suisse: profils et intégration, rather than the current reference-list Les musulmans de Suisse. Profil et intégration. Same three named authors and year support identity match; title difference retained.
original_2015_book_and_chain.data_provenance_evidence: The original project final report acquired from SNSF documents a representative survey fielded April–September 2009 among foreign Muslims from Turkey, Maghreb and Balkans plus non-Muslims. The author institution project page seen through web provider links that project to the 2015 book and lists 302 Turkish, 298 Maghrebians, 301 former-Yugoslavians and 305 non-Muslim Swiss. The direct institution HTTP fetch was a bot challenge, not the page contents.
original_2015_book_and_chain.supporting_secondary_evidence: Tunger-Zanetti’s 2016 review identifies the book as elaboration of the project’s 13-page 2010 outline and describes the same April–September 2009 survey: 1206 total, 901 Muslim foreigners and 305 non-Muslim Swiss. This corroborates project provenance but is not full original book inspection.
original_2015_book_and_chain.primary_related_finding: December 2010 project report, printed p.8, reports roughly one third feeling discriminated against on ethnic or religious grounds, with more Maghrebians reporting religious discrimination. Its displayed prose does not establish the exact 21/31/15 percentages or a 12-month recall period.
original_2015_book_and_chain.relationship_to_requested_gris2010: Evidence supports a distinct underlying survey from the 30 interviews in requested GRIS2010. The 2015 book is linked to an expanded report of a DIFFERENT 2010 document (Giugni/Gianni/Michel project report), not shown to be an expanded report of requested Gianni/Purdie/Lathion/Jenny2010.
original_2015_book_and_chain.relationship_limit: 2015 full empirical chapter unavailable: cannot exclude the book also citing/reusing older qualitative material; cannot directly verify its exact discrimination table, wording, denominators or all overlaps. Formal participant-level non-overlap cannot be certified.

original_2003.identity: Hong, Benet-Martínez, Chiu and Morris; Boundaries of Cultural Influence: Construct Activation as a Mechanism for Cultural Differences in Social Perception; JCCP 34(4), 453–464, July 2003.
original_2003.doi_discrepancy: Original first page prints 10.1177/0022022103254201 (Crossref request returned 404). Requested 10.1177/0022022103034004005 registers matching title/authors/journal/pages/year. No claim that the printed alternate DOI has been proven a registered alias.
original_2003.data_and_timeframe: Study 1: 120 Hong Kong Chinese undergraduates. Study 2: 100 Chinese-born UC Berkeley students, selected for at least five years in US and five years in a listed Chinese society. Exact collection dates not reported in inspected methods. Published July 2003 does not itself date observations.
original_2003.protocol: Study 1 randomly assigned American/Chinese/control primes: eight pictures plus writing ten sentences about culture/landscapes over 15 minutes. Four fish-cartoon presentations manipulate salience within participant: leading fish differs in colour from group versus matches it. Study 1 response is a 1–12 bipolar group/individual attribution confidence scale. Study 2 uses five pretested icons and a different low-salience display (each fish a different colour), and separate 9-point group and individual attribution scales.
original_2003.conditional_finding: The paper explicitly presents applicability as a previously untested boundary condition: American versus Chinese cultural priming affects attribution when individual/group agency is salient and does not when low-salience. Study 1 Priming×Salience F(2,118)=6.32, p<.01; Study 2 F(2,96)=4.31, p<.05, as printed.
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: In Study 2 the separate individual-attribution measure was nonsignificant in both salience conditions; significant conditional effect concerns group attribution.
Chinese-prime versus control differences were not reliable. Do not expand finding into every pairwise contrast or every attribution outcome.
The same Chinese primes had been used in prior 1997/2000 studies; shared stimuli establish continuity of paradigm, not data equivalence or independence.

closest_1997_report.identity_status: Bibliographic identity supported, but not verified from original chapter front page. AASP contents names Chapter 8 by Hong/Chiu/Tracy Man Kung; author lists it as 1997 Wiley edited-volume chapter.
closest_1997_report.conference_status: The containing volume is identified by the issuing association as proceedings of the inaugural 1995 Hong Kong conference. Thus conference-proceedings provenance is supported. This is not evidence that it is an early report of the 2003 data.
closest_1997_report.sample_and_finding_access_limit: Current article describes 1997 experiments 2 and 3, reports original Ns 303 and 75 in footnote 4, and describes three icon-prime groups and fish attribution task. These are current-author reports, not independently checked 1997 contents. No exact original field dates recovered.
closest_1997_report.same_data_as_2003: Not established. Full 2003 text distinguishes prior 1997/2000 accessibility work from its two applicability studies and explicitly says no prior study tested that principle. This is substantive evidence for a distinct conditional finding/protocol beyond generic priming. Without 1997 chapter contents, exact study/data reuse or participant overlap cannot be conclusively excluded.
closest_1997_report.bibliographic_variation: Current citation 135–146 versus Hong author publication list and 2003 references 139–150. Do not infer separate original studies from differing page citations.

current_experiments_4_6.design_link: Experiment 4 explicitly uses the 2003 high-salience image; Experiments 5 and 6 retain that approach while adjusting age/sample/language. Experiment 4: 2021, Dynata, N=565, ages 18–39; Experiment 5: 2022, classroom students and Lucid ages 18–25, N=451, English; Experiment 6: 2022, Dynata ages 18–65, N=522, Chinese.
current_experiments_4_6.scope_limit: These use the high-salience condition rather than re-running the complete high-versus-low factorial interaction. Outcomes are the current 12-point internal attribution scale and coded open explanations; not all 2003 measures. Power calculations still refer to 1997. No replication outcome adjudicated here.

quotes.text:
Regarding perception
of discrimination, while 8% of non-Muslims say that they
have felt discriminated against during the last 12 months,
16% of the Muslim respondents mention such feelings.
This variable is not taken into account in the explicative
analysis of unemployment, but it gives us a hint at the
situation of Muslims in Switzerland.

These findings replicate what other scholars have
found about Muslims in Switzerland (Gianni et al., 2015;
Gianni, Purdie, Lathion, & Jenny, 2010). The question is,
however, whether these differences also help to explain
the Muslim employment gap. To answer this question,
we now present the results of the logistic regressions predicting unemployment.

The most recent study points to the fact that nonSwiss Muslims feel discriminated amongst, with 21% of
Turks, 31% of North Africans, and 15% of ex-Yugoslavians
in the sample having had a feeling that they were discriminated against on the basis of their religion in the
past 12 months (Gianni et al., 2015).

La base empirique de cette étude porte sur
30 ­entretiens semi-directifs, sur la base d’une grille
d’entretien conçue pour aborder les thèmes susmentionnés 15 avec les personnes interrogées.16

Bien entendu, il ne nous est pas possible, par
cette étude, de mesurer l’ampleur de ce type de comportements et de discriminations. Il n’en demeure pas
moins qu’une partie importante des personnes inter­
rogées fait état, directement ou indirectement (par
exemple en se référant à des connaissances), de ce type
de phénomènes.

Car
la discrimination est présente, on parle de préjugés,
­d’incompréhension, mais également d’exclusion

Auteur
Matteo Gianni
avec la collaboration de Mallory Schneuwly Purdie, Stéphane Lathion, Magali Jenny
2e édition du rapport 2005, complétée de l’analyse de Stéphane Lathion
Le reste de l’étude a été repris tel quel.

Extrait du titre Les musulmans en Suisse - Profils et intégration
De Matteo Gianni, Marco Giugni et Noémi Michel
Publié aux Presses polytechniques et universitaires romandes

Il a été conduit entre avril et
septembre 2009 et s'est concentré sur les étrangers de confession musulmane et originaires de
Turquie, du Maghreb et des Balkans. Ces trois origines constituent en effet les régions de
provenance de la très grande majorité des musulmans résidents en Suisse.

Dans le cas des musulmans, une partie relativement importante de cette population
(environ 1/3 des répondants) a le sentiment d’avoir été discriminé en Suisse sur la base de
critères qui ont trait aux différences ethnique ou religieuse.
It is the worked-out research report of a project of which a 13-page outline had been published online in 2010.

However, no previous studies (to our knowledge) have
tested the applicability principle of knowledge activation in culture’s effect on cognition.

Participants were 120 Hong Kong Chinese undergraduates who had extensive knowledge
about Chinese culture and Western culture.

Participants were 100 Chinese-born students who attended UC Berkeley. They were selected
for having lived at least 5 years in the United States and at least 5 years in People’s Republic
of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macao, or Singapore.

Specifically, American cultural primes elicited
fewer attributions to the group in the high-salience but not the low-salience condition.

The priming effect on the
individual attribution measure, however, was not significant in either the high-salience condition or the low-salience condition.3

Therefore, in Experiment 4, we attempted a replication using the high

salience image used by Hong et al. (2003) (see Online Appendix 2).
Chapter 8–Bringing Culture Out in Front: Effects of Cultural Meaning System Activation on Social Cognition. Ying-yi Hong, Chi-yue Chiu and Tracy Man Kung
Proceedings of the Inaugural Conference of the Asian Association of Social Psychology 1995, Hong Kong

previous studies using the same Chinese cultural primes (Hong, Chiu, & Kung, 1997; Hong,
Morris, et al., 2000) have found reliable cultural knowledge activation effect.
